questions.q: For whom did Belshazzar, the king, make a great feast?
questions.a: He made a great feast for a thousand of his nobles.

questions.q: Who was this Belshazzar?
questions.a: He was the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar.

questions.q: What containers did they use to drink the wine from at this feast?
questions.a: They used the gold containers that had been taken out of the temple, the house of God, in Jerusalem.

questions.q: What did the people at the feast do as they drank the wine?
questions.a: They praised their idols made of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.

questions.q: As the people were drinking wine and praising their idols, what happened?
questions.a: The fingers of a human hand appeared in front of the lamp stand and wrote on the plaster wall in the king’s palace.

questions.q: What was the king’s immediate response when he saw the hand?
questions.a: His face turned pale, his thoughts terrified him, and his legs became so weak that his knees were shaking.

questions.q: What did the king promise to the one who could explain the writing on the plaster wall and its meaning?
questions.a: The king promised that the one who explained the writing and its meaning would be clothed in purple and would have a gold chain put around his neck and that he would have the authority of the third highest ruler in the kingdom.

questions.q: What happened when the king’s wise men came in to look at the writing?
questions.a: They were not able to read the writing or tell the king what it meant.

questions.q: What happened to King Belshazzar and his nobles when the wise men could not read the writing?
questions.a: The king became even more afraid and his face grew pale, and his nobles were confused and did not know what to do.

questions.q: Who came into the banquet hall because of what the king and his nobles were saying?
questions.a: The queen came in and told the king not to be afraid and not to let his face turn pale.

questions.q: According to the queen, what position did King Nebuchadnezzar give to this man?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar made him chief over the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and diviners.

questions.q: What did the queen tell the king to do?
questions.a: She told him to call for Daniel, because Daniel would show the king the interpretation of the writing.

questions.q: According to the king what qualities did he say he had heard about Daniel?
questions.a: The king said he had heard that the spirit of the gods was in Daniel, and that Daniel had light, understanding, and excellent wisdom.

questions.q: What did the king tell Daniel about his wise men?
questions.a: The king said his wise men had been brought in to read the writing, but they were not able to explain its interpretation.

questions.q: What did the king promise Daniel if he could read the writing and explain it?
questions.a: The king promised that Daniel would wear purple, have a gold chain around his neck, and rule as the third ruler in the kingdom.

questions.q: What was Daniel’s response when he was told of the rewards he would receive for reading the writing and explaining its meaning?
questions.a: Daniel told the king, “Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another person. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to you, king, and will tell you the meaning.”

questions.q: According to Daniel, who gave Nebuchadnezzar the kingdom, greatness, honor, and majesty?
questions.a: The Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar the kingdom, greatness, honor, and majesty.

questions.q: What could Nebuchadnezzar do to anyone he wished, according to Daniel?
questions.a: He could kill or let live anyone he wished, and he could lift up or humble anyone he wished.

questions.q: Why was Nebuchadnezzar brought down from his kingly throne and why was his majesty taken away from him?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar lost his majesty and his throne because his heart became arrogant and his spirit was hardened so that he acted presumptuously.

questions.q: Where did Nebuchadnezzar live after he was driven away from people?
questions.a: He lived among the wild donkeys and ate grass like oxen until he knew that the Most High God rules over human kingdoms.

questions.q: What were Daniel’s charges against Belshazzar?
questions.a: Daniel said Belshazzar had not humbled his heart, he had lifted himself up against the Lord of the heavens, and he had not honored the God who held his breath in his hand and who knew all his ways.

questions.q: According to Daniel, what was sent from God and wrote on the wall?
questions.a: The palm of a hand was sent from God, and it wrote the message on the wall.

questions.q: What words were written on the wall?
questions.a: The words were Mene, Mene, Tekel, and Parsin.

questions.q: What was the meaning of the writing on the plaster wall?
questions.a: The meaning was as follows: God has numbered Belshazzar’s kingdom and brought it to an end. Belshazzar is weighed in the scales and found deficient. Belshazzar’s kingdom is divided and is given to the Medes and Persians.

questions.q: What did Belshazzar do for Daniel after Daniel explained the writing?
questions.a: Belshazzar had Daniel clothed with purple and a gold chain around his neck, and proclaimed him the third ruler in the kingdom.

questions.q: What happened that night after Daniel gave his interpretation of the writing to Belshazzar?
questions.a: That night Belshazzar, the king of the Chaldeans, was killed, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom.

questions.q: How old was Darius the Mede when he received the kingdom?
questions.a: Darius the Mede was sixty-two years old when he received the kingdom.

commentary.text: Belshazzar's impious feast; the hand-writing on the wall. (Dan. 5:1-9) Daniel is sent for to interpret it. (Dan. 5:10-17) Daniel warns the king of his destruction. (Dan. 5:18-31)

Dan. 5:1-9 Belshazzar bade defiance to the judgments of God. Most historians consider that Cyrus then besieged Babylon. Security and sensuality are sad proofs of approaching ruin. That mirth is sinful indeed, which profanes sacred things; and what are many of the songs used at modern feasts better than the praises sung by the heathens to their gods! See how God struck terror upon Belshazzar and his lords. God's written word is enough to put the proudest, boldest sinner in a fright. What we see of God, the part of the hand that writes in the book of the creatures, and in the book of the Scriptures, should fill us with awful thoughts concerning that part which we do not see. If this be the finger of God, what is his arm when made bare? And what is He? The king's guilty conscience told him that he had no reason to expect any good news from heaven. God can, in a moment, make the heart of the stoutest sinner to tremble; and there needs no more than to let loose his own thoughts upon him; they will give him trouble enough. No bodily pain can equal the inward agony which sometimes seizes the sinner in the midst of mirth, carnal pleasures, and worldly pomp. Sometimes terrors cause a man to flee to Christ for pardon and peace; but many cry out for fear of wrath, who are not humbled for their sins, and who seek relief by lying vanities. The ignorance and uncertainty concerning the Holy Scriptures, shown by many who call themselves wise, only tend to drive sinners to despair, as the ignorance of these wise men did.

Dan. 5:10-17 Daniel was forgotten at court; he lived privately, and was then ninety years of age. Many consult servants of God on curious questions, or to explain difficult subjects, but without asking the way of salvation, or the path of duty. Daniel slighted the offer of reward. He spoke to Belshazzar as to a condemned criminal. We should despise all the gifts and rewards this world can give, did we see, as we may by faith, its end hastening on; but let us do our duty in the world, and do it all the real service we can.

Dan. 5:18-31 Daniel reads Belshazzar's doom. He had not taken warning by the judgments upon Nebuchadnezzar. And he had insulted God. Sinners are pleased with gods that neither see, nor hear, nor know; but they will be judged by One to whom all things are open. Daniel reads the sentence written on the wall. All this may well be applied to the doom of every sinner. At death, the sinner's days are numbered and finished; after death is the judgment, when he will be weighed in the balance, and found wanting; and after judgment the sinner will be cut asunder, and given as a prey to the devil and his angels. While these things were passing in the palace, it is considered that the army of Cyrus entered the city; and when Belshazzar was slain, a general submission followed. Soon will every impenitent sinner find the writing of God's word brought to pass upon him, whether he is weighed in the balance of the law as a self-righteous Pharisee, or in that of the gospel as a painted hypocrite.
